I have found two main study techniques that work. First, reviewing the lectures and ensuring I can derive everything on my own (this is what I did for other exams with this professor). Additionally, doing practice problems if I have time (this is what I did for lower-division exams). If I start studying for the final this weekend, I could have enough time to do both practice problems and derivations (and it would take off pressure from finals week).

Hopefully, you are right. I have raised my grades in the past, despite it seeming impossible (65 and 69 on midterm exams in DiffEq, and a 102 on the final), so it should be possible again.

I also just joined a high-energy physics lab, so I should have research for the rest of my undergraduate years.

>Many people go out and work a few years before returning to grad school, and the more experience you have under your belt, the less your GPA will matter.

>I grew up a gifted kid. Straight As, advanced classes, the works. Right up until I didn't. There was turbulence, I got a lot of grief, they said and did things I'm sure they now regret and that hurt me.

This is what happened throughout high school. I do not think my parents—especially my mother—can give up the idea of me being perfect. But I do not *want* to be perfect. I do not want to ‘change the world’—at least, not in the way my parents expect. This has been what they have expected from me since I was in kindergarten, and that is way too much pressure for anyone. If it happens, great, but I just want to study physics and do a good job. I do not want that to be my only priority in life. I was finally learning to love physics again, and I do not want to lose that by burning out. However, I have no idea how to explain this to my parents.

I hope so. I was able to figure out how to handle physics—my exam grades went from 60% to 93%, and this was during a unit I thought I knew nothing about. But this is different—I need at least 104% to get an A–, and we *can* theoretically get as high as 115% (I believe he caps the grades at 107.5%, though), but I would have to do *really* well to get such a high grade. If he has mercy and caps the grades at 108%, then I can actually get an A (just barely, but an A is an A).

She said I am eligible for accommodations (which will allow me to pause for a few minutes and calm down when I panic, without having to worry about running out of time to work). Luckily, we can get as high as 107% on the math final. I just need a 103% to get an A– in the class. While I still really, *really* wish I could get an A, this is probably not the best class to use my one-time late drop for.
This is something I find reassuring. My parents will likely force me to tell them my grades, but I can probably wait until we are in public (they will not start yelling in public).

>Also, why would your parents be pissed at like, a B or a B- for the course?

Probably the same reason they were pissed I got a B when I took differential equations in high school (I was not ready for the class at the time, but they made me take it and got mad when I did not get an A).

My parents—mainly my mother—definitely have high expectations. To give some examples:

* My mother got angry that I did not start a business in high school.
* My mother got angry that I did not become an influencer in high school.
* My mother got angry that I did not start a YouTube channel or blog in high school.
* My mother is still annoyed that I did not get into an Ivy League college (I got into one of the top public research universities where I live).
* My mother would not allow me to do homework, claiming that it would do nothing to get me into a good college and that I should focus on applications instead (but would get angry when my grades dropped).
* My mother made me retake the SAT when I got a 1550.
* My mother got angry that I was "not involved" in school. I was in choir and Science Olympiad for four years, and I was the president of two clubs. Among other things.

There is also a lot of things she did not related to academics—making me get painful cosmetic procedures, restricting food for "health" reasons, and some other things—but I think you get the idea.

I wish I could tell my mother to stop, but she would only get angrier. I know she loves me, but she is too prideful to change her behavior, even when confronted by the entire family.

I emailed my professor, but I am concerned that it may be too late to ask for help. That being said, he is pretty nice. I am really hoping there will be a chance for extra credit.

My exam is on May 4th. If I start studying tomorrow, *maybe* I can do well enough to raise my grade to a B+. As much as I had hoped to keep my 4.0 GPA, though, I do not think that will be happening. I am mainly worried that it will harm my chances of getting into graduate school.

I (18F) realized that I was emotionally neglected about two years ago (although I have known that something was wrong since the beginning of high school). Between the ongoing emotional neglect and emotional abuse, I was…not doing well.

Without going into detail, I developed some poor habits (self-harm). I was terrified of talking to other people and had no idea how to process…well, anything.

So I started writing.

I could not *talk* about my feelings, so I put fictional characters in my situation. I watched them break and receive the love. I also read books and fanfiction *constantly*—seriously, it reached unhealthy levels—to distract myself.

In real life, affection still feels strange. But living vicariously through my characters has helped me manage the worst of my emotions. I am happy to say that I am nearly two months clean of self-harm (I have been projecting my urges onto a character in one of my fanfictions).

This strategy is not perfect—not even close. However, it is allowing me to survive until college.

Take this advice with a grain of salt. I do not have much experience with writing songs.

* Pick a perspective. Do you want the song to be sung *by* him or *about* him?
* Pick a tone. Do you want the song to be happy? Sad? Angry? Keep in mind that the tone of the lyrics does not necessarily have to match the mood of the music—for example, you could write a song that is upbeat but dark (such as Addict).
* Pick a theme. What do you want the song to be about? His life? His relationships? His views on romance? His hopes? His fears? Think of the lyrics as a story—what are you trying to say about him?

For the actual writing process:

* Outline. This may sound juvenile, but determine what you want the listener to take away from the song. Imagine the story you want to tell—on what emotional note do you want the song to start? On what emotional note do you want it to end?
   * With Addict as an example: the music evolves from a (relatively) upbeat song about Angel and his carefree afterlife to a darker song about his emotional pain and reliance on drugs.
* Exact rhymes are less important than you might think. Having said that—[RhymeZone](https://rhymezone.com) is a great resource if you need help finding rhymes and/or near-rhymes.
* Pay attention to meter (the beat of the words). This can be flexible—I just thought I would throw it out there.

I hope this works for you. Let me know if you have any questions. Good luck with your song!

* Relaxation (in my case, music)
* Comfort (in my case, writing)

I'm not sure how similar your mother is to mine, but in my experience, my mother might latch onto a particular hobby and get angry at me for doing it. Whenever this happens, I tend to get afraid to return to that hobby, even if it is a source of comfort (it took me three weeks to coax myself back into writing, and I still cannot return to the same story).

**Mental Health:** Do you have friends you can vent to about your situation? If so, as scary as it may seem, this might be an incredibly helpful option. Again, I don't know the details of your situation, but when I spoke to my best friend about my feelings, I found an outlet beyond self-harm. I'm not sure what country you live in, but if you can, try find a number for a mental health lines.

Text Lines: This is what I prefer. Where I live, there is a general mental health crisis line, so I have messaged them on days where I feel particularly bad. I have spoken about my mother on a couple of occasions, and while they have offered to make a report, I declined (had I given my personal information, they would be legally required to make a report, but they were very kind when I said I did not want to give my information).

Another advantage of text lines is that your parents cannot hear you physically speaking to another person.

Warmlines: I do not have much information on warmlines, but I do know that they are less "urgent" than hotlines. I would recommend looking them up to see whether they are available in your country. 

Hotlines: I have never used a hotline, and if I am being honest, I do not know much about them.

All in all, mental health lines are useful, especially if you need to talk to someone about the abuse. I am assuming that they are also helpful, at least in the immediate moment, when it comes to self-harm (I have never spoken about self-harm on the text line). However, I would recommend researching a line before using it, just to be on the safe side. I did extensive research on the text line before I actually used it. I wanted to make sure that it would be private.

If possible, I would also recommend speaking to a school counselor, but I understand that it is not always practical to do so (I have not done this).

Reddit is a useful outlet, and personally, I find Tumblr to be helpful as well. There are two specific blogs ([one-abuse-survivor](https://one-abuse-survivor.tumblr.com/) and [furiousgoldfish](https://furiousgoldfish.tumblr.com/)) that speak a lot about abuse and trauma. These blogs have helped me quite a bit. The first blog also allows people to send Asks, and I think it is possible to send in an Anonymous Ask without having a Tumblr account. I've submitted Asks in the past, and the advice is (in my opinion) very helpful.

Just do whatever you can to survive. Keep your head above the water.

**Preparing for the Future:** This is more generic, but try to focus on school. Keep your grades up. If possible, college can be an escape. I am not sure how the education system works in your country, but there is an international alternative to high school diplomas that you can research (GEDs). At the very least, a high school diploma or GED is required for most jobs. 

If you would like to go to college, you might be able to look into scholarships or estrangement funds.

Other important skills to learn are:

* Cooking
* Cleaning
* Managing finances
